There are still spaces available on board three Fred. Olsen cruises which will journey to Norway for aurora hunting, husky sledding, cable car riding and more

The Northern Lights have been making an appearance in the North East once again this autumn, and their spectacular ribbons of colour dancing across the night sky is simply something that everyone should see at least once in their lifetime. Those who want to take their aurora hunting to the next level can book an unforgettable trip to do so from the Port of Tyne early next year.

Fred. Olsen is offering three In Search Of The Northern Lights cruises sailing from Tyneside in February and March 2027, coinciding with the time of year when aurora displays are typically at their most frequent. These 10-night holidays will journey into the Arctic Circle via the dramatic coastline of Norway, offering passengers the best opportunity to witness a colourful show.

The abundance of Northern Lights events in recent years is due to the sun going through a period of increased activity called Solar Maximum. With this thought to have reached its peak in 2024, the verdict from experts is that it causes elevated aurora activity for one to three years afterwards, so 2027 could be the last time for several years that Northern Lights chasers are most likely to see a show.

Arctic adventures from sled rides to cable cars

The first of the three In Search of the Northern Lights cruises is also Fred. Olsen's first departure from the Port of Tyne in 2027, setting sail on February 22. With ocean view cabins available to book online from £2,449 per person, this journey invites guests to cosy up on deck with a blanket and hot chocolate as the Bolette ship crosses the Arctic Circle, where they will be "perfectly placed" to see any aurora that light up the dark skies above.

Meanwhile, five ports of call across Norway offer passengers the opportunity to immerse themselves in an Arctic adventure, from taking husky sled rides through the snow to seeing reindeer roaming the wintry wilderness. Panoramic views of snow-speckled islands and fjords can be seen at the top of Mount Aksla in Alesund, while in Tromso - the only one of the three Northern Lights cruises to visit the city - cable car rides offer yet more opportunity to witness the breathtaking surrounding scenery.

Overnight stay for aurora hunting in Norway

The next In Search of the Northern Lights cruise sailing from the Port of Tyne on March 4 has Ocean View rooms available from £1,819 per person, although this trip has four stops on its itinerary rather than five. Stopping off in Alesund, Sortland and Molde, this 10-night cruise also includes an overnight stay in Harstad, offering holidaymakers the chance to find more adventures ashore from snowshoe hiking by day to Northern Lights seeking by night.

Rounding off the trio is the final In Search of the Northern Lights cruise sailing on March 14, which will see passengers aboard during the spring equinox on March 20. The Northern Lights are typically at their most active during the spring and autumn equinoxes that occur in March and September respectively, as the way that the Earth is tilted on its axis during these periods opens up 'cracks' in the magnetic field which allows solar winds to enter our atmosphere more than they would at other times of the year.

With remaining cabins starting from £1,849 per person for ocean view rooms, this trip crosses the Arctic Circle following its first stop in Alesund, journeying on to Harstad, Sortland, Narvik and Molde. Alternatively, for those hoping to see the Northern Lights who don't have the cash to splash on a cruise, there are a few destinations available to jet off to from Newcastle Airport.

More Northern Lights adventures from Newcastle

According to Nordic Visitor, the best places to see the aurora are the Nordic countries of Iceland, Norway, Sweden and Finland, which lie within or near the Arctic Circle. Flights run from Newcastle to the Icelandic capital of Reykjavik on Wednesdays and Sundays in the months of October and November as well as in February, March and April via Jet2, priced from £44 per person.

Holidaymakers can also travel from Newcastle to the cities of Stavanger and Bergen in Norway directly with Loganair, although from here they may have to travel further north to be in with the best chance of seeing the Northern Lights. And there are multiple departures to Lapland in Finland during November and December with TUI, easyJet, Transun, Santa's Lapland, and Canterbury Travel for the ultimate Christmas break, as well as in January and March.

It's worth bearing in mind, however, that the Northern Lights are not like weather - they are notoriously difficult to predict in advance due to the number of conditions that must align for them to occur. An aurora display can only be forecast couple of days at most before it hits, and even then the forecast can change multiple times per day depending on a number of shifting factors.

There is also a great deal of luck involved in catching a Northern Lights display, with clear skies required - the aurora unfortunately cannot be seen through clouds - and times when the moon is not full are best, as its brightness can impact the visibility of an aurora. It must also be dark, making the long nights of winter the perfect opportunity, but holidaymakers should be aware that a show is never guaranteed.
